verses.translation_literal: A song of the ascents. To you I have lifted up my eyes, the one who sits in the heavens.
verses.translation_dramatic: A song for the climbing road. To you, only to you, I lift my eyes, to you who sit enthroned in the heavens, high above every hand that could reach me.
verses.directors_commentary:
This is the first line of a pilgrim's song, one of the fifteen Songs of the Ascents, sung by travelers going up to Jerusalem, which sits on its ridge some 750 metres above the sea. The speaker lifts the eyes, not a bowed head or a hidden face: this is the posture of someone with nowhere else to look. The singer says 'I' while the next verses say 'we', so one voice is carrying a whole people. Play it as a gaze that goes up past the hills, past every human patron, to a throne.

The Hebrew calls God 'the one who sits' (הַיֹּשְׁבִי), a verb of enthronement: a king sits to rule and to judge. Here the KJV softens it. 'Thou that dwellest in the heavens' turns a throne into a residence, and Webster follows it with 'dwellest'; YLT's 'dweller' goes the same way. The ASV's 'sittest' keeps the Hebrew picture, and BBE's 'whose seat is' catches it too. The final yod on the participle is an archaic or poetic ending, which Rashi, Radak, Meiri and Metzudat Zion all note as an extra letter; it adds no meaning, but it lends the line a solemn, old-fashioned ring. The KJV also drops 'the' before 'ascents': 'degrees' is the old word for steps, so the title means the steps up to the Temple, or the going up of the pilgrims.

philological_notes.note: The participle 'the one who sits', with an extra final yod that Rashi, Radak, Meiri and Metzudat Zion all call superfluous (Meiri compares it to המגביהי and המשפילי). The verb ישב is used of kings enthroned and judges seated, so 'sits' is more than 'lives'. KJV and Webster 'dwellest' make it a residence.

'I have lifted my eyes': the idiom of looking up in expectation or appeal. The perfect tense can be read as a present, 'I lift', as ASV and KJV do, or as an act already done and still going on, as YLT does. Malbim reads it as looking to God alone, not to natural means.

'The ascents', a plural of מַעֲלָה, from the root 'to go up'. It is the heading of Psalms 120 to 134. Whether it means the pilgrim road up to Jerusalem or the steps of the Temple is not settled; KJV's 'degrees' is the Latin-derived word for steps. My own reading follows the pilgrim sense.

verses.translation_literal: Behold, like the eyes of slaves to the hand of their masters, like the eyes of a slave woman to the hand of her mistress, so our eyes [are] to YHWH our God, until he shows us favor.
verses.translation_dramatic: Look: as the servants watch the hand of their master, as the maid watches the hand of her mistress — for the lift, the sign, the blow held back — so our eyes are fixed on the LORD our God, and they will not leave him until he shows us favor.
verses.directors_commentary:
The image is two eyes fixed on a hand. In a household economy the hand of the master gives the bread, points the task, or strikes; a slave watches it constantly because nothing is spoken that the hand does not first show. Radak says slaves have no living or food except from their masters, so their eyes hang on them; Meiri adds that when the owner is about to strike, the slave has no one else to look to but the owner, and begs for the hand to be relaxed. Malbim finds a further layer: the mistress passes on what she receives from the master, so the double picture covers both God as source and God as the one who hands it on. Play the psalmists as people with no recourse at all, not as eager servants.

The KJV's 'servants' and 'maiden' are polite words. עֲבָדִים is slaves, and שִׁפְחָה is a female slave, the woman at the very bottom of the household. 'Wait upon' in the KJV makes it sound like attendance; the Hebrew just says 'our eyes are to YHWH', and it keeps the preposition 'to' from the first half. The last word, שֶׁיְּחָנֵּנוּ, 'until he shows us favor', is the same root (חנן) that the next verse doubles. The KJV and ASV's 'have mercy' is close but the root is the free, undeserved favor of a superior. Notice also that the first line used God as 'one who sits' in heaven; here the sitter is the master with a hand, and the gaze has become the stance of a slave.

philological_notes.note: Literally 'to the hand of'. The hand is the active part of the master: it feeds or strikes. Radak and Meiri explain the image as dependence on food and as pleading for a held-back blow; Metzudat David says the servants watch the hand to be given something.
A female slave, lower in the household than the mistress; the KJV's 'maiden' is a softening.
'Her mistress', the lady of the house, the master's wife; Metzudat Zion compares Sarai's 'my mistress' (Genesis 16:8; he cites it as chapter 17).

verses.translation_literal: Show us favor, YHWH, show us favor, for much we have been sated [with] contempt.
verses.translation_dramatic: Be gracious to us, LORD — be gracious! We have had our fill, and more than our fill, of contempt.
verses.directors_commentary:
The first request is repeated, and the name of God sits between the two cries like a hinge. Radak says the doubling strengthens the plea; the Targum doubles it too. After the quiet gaze of verse 2 this is the first spoken request, and it should break out of the silence, short, with no preparation, then again, lower.

The reason is a hunger image turned upside down. שָׂבַעְנוּ is the word for being full after a meal, for being sated. Here the people have been fed to the point of nausea with בּוּז, contempt. The KJV's 'exceedingly filled with contempt' is fair, but BBE's 'all men are looking down on us' flattens the feast to a description. Hold the word 'sated' with disgust, as one speaks after a meal one did not choose. Ibn Ezra takes רַב as 'for a long time' (we have been full of it for ages), the usual translations as 'exceedingly'; the Hebrew word can carry both, and the literal line keeps it simple. Contempt, בּוּז, is not abstract, it is the sound of being laughed at by those who are comfortable, which the next verse names.

philological_notes.note: Imperative 'show us favor, be gracious to us' with a pronoun suffix, repeated for force. The root names an undeserved favor from a superior; Radak sees the doubling as strengthening the request.
'We have been sated' — normally used of food. Metzudat David says contempt came to us in such quantity that we were sated, and calls this a figure of speech.

verses.translation_literal: Much has our soul been sated for itself — the mockery of the at-ease, the contempt of the arrogant oppressors.
verses.translation_dramatic: Long, too long, has our soul been fed on it: the laughter of the comfortable, the sneer of the proud, the weight of those who rule us and look down.
verses.directors_commentary:
The sentence builds by stacking. First the soul, נֶפֶשׁ, which is more than the 'self': it is the throat and the appetite and the person. It has been sated 'for itself', a dative that makes the point that the soul has filled itself with this, as if it had no other food. Then two nouns hang one on the other without a connector: 'the mockery, the at-ease' and 'the contempt, the arrogant ones'. Radak and Meiri explain the first by an elided head noun, 'the mockery [of] the at-ease', with parallels like 'the ark [of] the covenant' (Joshua 3:14); Ibn Ezra reads it the same way. The second pair, הַבּוּז לִגְאֵי יוֹנִים, is built the same way, with the unusual lamed that Meiri compares with 2 Kings 7:2.

The at-ease, הַשַּׁאֲנַנִּים, are people who live in comfort and security. The word is used for the quiet confidence of Moab in Jeremiah 48 (Metzudat Zion's example), and the mockery of someone who has never needed anything from anyone is the worst kind. The KJV's 'those that are at ease' is accurate; 'the proud' for the last phrase loses the written/read difference. The Hebrew text is written as one word, לגאיונים, and read as two, לגאי יונים. Rashi records this directly; Ibn Ezra and Radak treat the written word as a form like עליונים, from גאה, 'be proud'; Metzudat Zion derives it from גאוה 'pride' and אונאה 'oppression'. Rashi's reading of the second word as the 'valley of the yonim', that is Jerusalem, is homiletic and you should not play it. Play instead a mockery that comes down from above, from the comfortable to the poor and from the proud to the pressed.

philological_notes.note: Written as one word לגאיונים (Ketiv), read as two (Qere). Rashi records the split; Ibn Ezra and Radak take the one-word form as a formation like עליונים, from גאה 'be proud'; Metzudat Zion derives it from גאוה 'pride' and אונאה 'oppression'. Read as two words it is 'to the arrogant, the oppressors' (יונים from ינה, 'oppress'). The lamed marks a construct-like link (compare 2 Kings 7:2, as Meiri says).
'The at-ease, the carefree', those living undisturbed and secure. Metzudat Zion links it to the quiet of Moab in Jeremiah 48:11; Metzudat David links it to the people of Babylon.
'Much' or 'long': Ibn Ezra reads it as a measure of time ('for a long time'), Meiri as 'a long time'; the sense 'to excess' is also open.

token_glosses.gloss: of the arrogant ones, the oppressors
